summary: IODEF is an XML format for sharing information about computer security incidents. This document defines a way for its Reference class to point to entries in enumerations such as vulnerability lists, so an incident report can cite a specific known weakness in a standard way.

eli5.summary: When reporting a computer attack, you can say which known weakness was used. This makes a standard way to write down that label.

questions: how to reference cve in iodef
what is the iana security external enumeration registry
subtitle: A standard way for an incident report to say which kind of identifier it cites, such as a CVE number.

tldr.problem: IODEF incident reports can cite outside identifiers such as vulnerability numbers, but the Reference class gives a reader no reliable way to tell which enumeration an identifier comes from or how to parse it.
tldr.mechanism: A ReferenceName element carries a required integer specIndex that points into a new IANA registry of enumerations, plus a child ID element holding the value itself.
tldr.outcome: Reports can name both the enumeration and the entry in it in one structured form, and new enumerations can be added through the registry.

today: RFC 7495 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not update IODEF v1 (RFC 5070), but the format is used in IODEF v2.

sections.title: The Problem with Bare Identifiers
sections.content:
The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) is an XML framework for sharing information about computer security incidents. Its Reference class points to external information such as a vulnerability, an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) alert, a malware sample, an advisory or an attack technique.

In practice these references use external enumeration specifications, which define both the format of an identifier and its values. IODEF v1 (RFC 5070) types the ReferenceName as ML_STRING, so an implementer cannot tell whether a string is from the Common Vulnerability Enumeration (CVE), the Common Configuration Enumeration (CCE), the Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) or something else, and so how to parse it.

This document sets a required structure for ReferenceName, and uses an IANA registry to manage the enumerations. The format is used in IODEF v2, which the RFC says will replace IODEF v1. This document does not specify its use in IODEF v1.
sections.eli5: If someone says "number 1234", you ask, 1234 of what? This gives reports a standard way to say which list the number comes from.

sections.title: The ReferenceName Class
sections.content:
The ReferenceName class identifies an enumeration and gives a value from it. It has one required attribute, specIndex, an INTEGER that picks the enumeration. Each value must match the SpecIndex of an entry in the "Enumeration Reference Type Identifiers" IANA registry.

Its one child, ID, holds the identifier of the specific enumeration object being referenced. The format of the ID is given in the registry entry for that enumeration. The RFC's own example is a CVE-style identifier, CVE-2014-0001, which has a specific format and relates to information about one vulnerability.
sections.eli5: A ReferenceName is a label with two parts: a number saying which list you mean, and the actual item from that list.

sections.title: An Example Reference
sections.content:
The RFC shows a Reference that uses a made-up enumeration, "Concept X Identifier", registered in an imagined table as SpecIndex 1, version any, with a specification URI. The Reference holds the ReferenceName with its ID, a URL and a description.

A reader who sees specIndex="1" looks it up in the registry, finds how the ID is formatted and parses CXI-1234-XYZ accordingly.
sections.eli5: The report says "list number 1, item CXI-1234-XYZ". You look up list 1 to learn what such an item means.

sections.title: Use Beyond IODEF
sections.content: Although the document's scope is IODEF, any standard that needs to reference an enumeration identified by a specially formatted string can use the method after that standard is published. The RFC describes this as a standardized interface for enumeration formats, giving a loose coupling between a standard and the enumeration identifiers it needs to reference now and in the future.
sections.eli5: Any other rulebook that needs to point at items in outside lists can borrow the same labelling trick.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA created and maintains the "Security External Enumeration Registry". All fields are mandatory:

  • Full Name: the name of the enumeration or referenced specification, in printable ASCII with single embedded spaces.
  • Abbreviation: at least two uppercase letters (2*UC-ALPHA). Several registrations MAY share an abbreviation but MUST have different versions.
  • SpecIndex: an IANA-assigned positive integer. The first entry uses 1 and the value increments with each new entry.
  • Version: a free-form printable ASCII string without white space.
  • Specification URI/Reference: one or more URIs from which the specification can be obtained. It MUST be readily and publicly available. The URI SHOULD be stable and for a specific version; URIs for the latest version SHOULD NOT be used.

The initial content is Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, abbreviation CVE, SpecIndex 1, version 1.0. The allocation policy is Specification Required, which implies Expert Review. The Designated Expert is expected to consult the MILE (Managed Incident Lightweight Exchange) working group or its successor, check that the name, abbreviation and version are appropriate, ensure the specification is sufficient to parse identifiers unambiguously, and prefer short abbreviations over long ones.

The RFC also registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-enum-1.0 and the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:iodef-enum-1.0.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the master list of lists. Each entry gets a number, a name, a version and a place to read its rules, and the first entry is the CVE list.

sections.title: The XML Schema
sections.content: The schema defines a ReferenceName element in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-enum-1.0. It is a sequence containing one ID element of type xs:NCName, plus a required specIndex attribute of type xs:integer.
sections.eli5: The schema is the strict form that says a label must have a list number and an item name, and nothing else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mapping each ID to the correct SpecIndex matters. A wrong mapping gives inaccurate references and spreads misinformation. Enumeration reference IDs from trusted sources are preferred, though trust decisions are outside the scope of the document. Receiving an IODEF document with an unknown ReferenceName, where the SpecIndex is not in the IANA table, may indicate a misled or malicious source.

The enumeration's format is likely not a privacy concern, although the value may hold information that relying parties consider private. A Reference that combines an enumeration value with other data could expose information, such as attack vectors or system descriptions in a privacy-related incident. For protecting IODEF documents in transit and at rest, the RFC points readers to the Security Considerations of IODEF (RFC 5070).
sections.eli5: If the list number is wrong, people get the wrong facts. And a report that points to a list nobody knows about might come from someone untrustworthy.
